one_line_contribution: That retrieved agent memory injects a query-independent action prior — the block's action histogram copied onto the policy irrespective of state — and that removing it requires a per-retrieval probe estimate (MAC), which the paper claims will beat both scalar context scaling (CFG/CAD) and a fixed bank-level base-rate offset on ALFWorld.
closest_prior_work: Zhao et al. 2021 (Calibrate Before Use) plus the calibration successors the proposal already cites — and it concedes the mechanism. The residual novelty rests entirely on the assertion in Related Work that 'in classic ICL the demonstration set is fixed across the evaluation, so a single global offset suffices, and no prior calibration paper has had to answer whether adaptivity buys anything.' That assertion is the weakest sentence in the submission and I do not accept it. Retrieval-based ICL (Liu et al. 2022 KATE; Rubin et al. 2022 EPR) has had per-query-varying demonstration sets since 2022, and Zhao's probe is defined *relative to the current prompt* — recomputing it when the prompt changes per query is a re-run of the same equation, not a new estimator. Batch Calibration (Zhou et al. 2023) already estimates the bias adaptively at inference from the current batch rather than from a fixed global offset, and Domain-Context Calibration (Fei et al. 2023) already re-estimates it from in-domain content rather than a static content-free string. So the 'global bank base-rate offset' in E5(v) is not what the calibration literature actually prescribes under retrieval; it is a degraded variant the proposal has constructed to lose. If MAC beats it (P4), the finding is 'the textbook application of a 2021 method beats a variant nobody proposed'; if it ties, the proposal pre-commits to the title 'classic contextual calibration transfers unchanged'. Both branches of the novelty-bearing prediction land below an ICLR main-track bar.
strongest_objection: The confirmatory design has no established dynamic range, so P3 and P4 are close to arithmetically unwinnable. Every arm in E5 — MAC, CFG@γ*, the global offset, k=2, instruction debiasing — is a correction applied to the *same* uncalibrated k=4 injection, so the spread between any two of them is bounded above by the total effect of that injection relative to no-memory. The proposal never bounds that quantity: E0's gate only asks that injection 'moves ALFWorld success beyond the measured noise floor in either direction,' i.e. it can pass at ~3-4 points, and the antecedent pilot it leans on reports memory breaking six to seven items in absolute counts, not a large percentage swing. If uncalibrated injection costs, say, 3 points, then no two corrections can differ by the ≥4 points P3 and P4 demand, and both headline predictions fail for reasons that have nothing to do with whether the factorisation is real. The paper then reports 'parity' three times and concludes something it did not test. Second, the rescue from this is invalid as written: the 'pre-registered secondary, higher-power outcome' of ~30,000 *paired* decision steps with MDE ≈ 0.9 does not exist. Conditions share an initial state, but the moment MAC and CFG select different actions the episodes occupy different environment states, and every subsequent step is unpaired. McNemar on step-level executed-action correctness across 30 steps × 1,000 games is therefore not a paired test after the first divergence; the genuinely paired sample is the first divergent step plus whatever re-converges by luck, which is far smaller and non-randomly selected (episodes that never diverge contribute all their steps and zero signal, inflating concordance and deflating the apparent MDE). Third, no prediction requires MAC to beat the no-memory floor. E5 includes condition (i), but P3-P5 only pit MAC against other memory-using arms, so the paper can declare a double dissociation while every memory condition sits below no-memory — which is exactly what the pilot (zero fixes, six-to-seven breaks) predicts.
what_would_fix_it: (1) Make E0 a quantitative gate, not a directional one: measure |uncalibrated k=4 − no-memory| on the 200-game validation split first, and re-derive the P3/P4 thresholds as a stated fraction of that measured range rather than fixing them at ≥4 points a priori; if the range is under ~6 points, the confirmatory grid as designed cannot separate the arms and should be redesigned (e.g. larger k, or a domain where injection does more damage) before the 5,500 episodes are spent. (2) Add MAC > no-memory as a pre-registered gating contrast ahead of P3/P4 — without it, 'calibrated memory' can win the dissociation while losing to using no memory at all. (3) Drop the claim of 30,000 paired steps; replace it with the analysis the proposal already knows how to do — teacher-forced scoring of both conditions on *identical* held-out states (the E1 machinery) — plus a first-divergence-anchored outcome (does the first differing action agree with the expert plan) that is honestly paired at n = number of divergent episodes. (4) Replace the 'global bank base-rate offset' with the strong form of the static competitor: Zhao's content-free probe computed once on a *fixed* injected block, so that the comparison is adaptivity-vs-nonadaptivity at matched estimator quality rather than probe-vs-marginal. (5) Run the eight pre-committed queries before submission; a third failed search should postpone the paper, not be disclosed and proceeded past.
missing_baseline: A fixed-block memory arm: the same, non-retrieved injected block (matched token count and bank-representative action mix) used for every query and every step. This is the actual control for the entire adaptivity claim — it is the condition under which a single global correction is provably sufficient, and comparing it against retrieved k=4 is what establishes that per-query histogram variation costs anything in the first place. Without it, E0's JSD/drift statistics are descriptive only and P4 tests estimator quality rather than adaptivity. Secondary omissions a reviewer will also demand: an oracle/upper-bound arm (subtract the *true* per-block action marginal computed by averaging over held-out real states, i.e. E2c's estimator used as the correction rather than only as a validity check) to bound how much of the harm any calibration can recover; and MAC applied on top of k=2 volume reduction, since the pilot already showed k=2 neutralises the harm and the paper never tests whether MAC adds anything to the cheap fix it must beat.
preprint_collision: The check is not thin — it is empty, and by the proposal's own admission for the second consecutive round: zero results returned, tool failure, 'no verified closest recent work and no verified gap.' The proposal deserves credit for saying so plainly rather than dressing up silence as novelty, and for enumerating exact future queries and graceful-degradation branches (a)/(b)/(c). But an unsearched novelty claim is a weakness, and here it compounds with a conceded four-year-old mechanism: the entire remaining contribution sits in the two areas the proposal itself lists as 'materially likely' collisions — frequency/majority bias in LLM tool selection, and calibrated/contrastive decoding applied to agentic memory. It also flags branch (c), per-retrieval calibration under RAG-style variable demonstrations, under which 'the novelty claim collapses to the agentic/sequential transfer.' I judge branch (c) as already partly realised by indexed work rather than a hypothetical preprint risk: retrieval-conditioned demonstration selection plus contextual calibration is a documented combination, and Batch Calibration is an explicitly inference-time-adaptive bias estimate. So the collision risk is not merely unverified, it is unverified on top of an indexed threat the proposal mischaracterises. I cannot name a specific 2025-2026 arXiv preprint from within the constraints of this review, and I will not invent one — but the burden is the authors', and after two failed searches it remains entirely unmet.
